component gives
\[
 (P_{t_j}^{(d)}*\nu)(A_j)\ge c_dw_j,
\]
whereas, since \(t_j/R_j\to0\), the centred reference satisfies
\[
 P_{t_j}^{(d)}(A_j)
 \le C_d(t_j/R_j)^{d+1}
 =C_d\kappa^{d+1}w_j.
\]
Choose \(\kappa\) so that the second constant is strictly smaller than the
first.  Data processing to the partition \(\{A_j,A_j^c\}\) and
Lemma~\ref{lem:bernoulli-kl-linear-separation} then give
\(H_d(t_j)\ge c'_dw_j\).  Hence
\[
 t_j^4H_d(t_j)
 \ge c''_dR_j^4w_j^{1+4/(d+1)}
 =c''_d\alpha_j^{1+4/(d+1)}
 R_j^{2(d-3)/(d+1)}.
\]
The exponent of \(R_j\) is positive exactly when \(d>3\).  Choosing the
radii recursively makes the final expression tend to infinity.
\end{proof}

For the high-dimensional entropy topology, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-kl-exponents}
 q_d:=\frac{d+5}{d+1},
 \qquad
 p_d:=\frac{4(d+1)}{d+5}.
\end{equation}
Thus \(1<q_d<2\), \(2<p_d<4\), and \(p_dq_d=4\) when \(d\ge4\).

\begin{lemma}[Critical translation remainder]
\label{lem:critical-lq-translation-remainder}
Let \(d\ge4\), let \(p_d,q_d\) be as in
\eqref{eq:critical-kl-exponents}, and put \(m=\lfloor p_d\rfloor\).
If \(T_m(y,z)\) is the Taylor polynomial of \(F_y(z)\) through degree
\(m\), then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-lq-exact-translation-norm}
 \|F_\cdot(z)\|_{L^{q_d}(\Omega_d)}^{q_d}
 =1+\frac{2(d+5)}{(d+1)(d+3)}|z|^2
 +\frac{3}{(d+1)(d+3)}|z|^4.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for a constant depending only on \(d\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-lq-global-remainder}
 \|F_\cdot(z)-T_m(\cdot,z)\|_{L^{q_d}(\Omega_d)}
 \le C_d
 \begin{cases}
 |z|^{m+1},& |z|\le1,\\
 |z|^{p_d},& |z|>1,
 \end{cases}
 \le C_d|z|^{p_d}.
\end{equation}
Here \(m=2\) for \(4\le d\le10\), while \(m=3\) for \(d\ge11\),
including the integer endpoint \(p_{11}=3\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since \(a(q_d-1)=2\), translation by \(z\) gives
\[
 \|F_\cdot(z)\|_{q_d}^{q_d}
 =c_d\int_{\RR^d}
 \frac{(1+|u+z|^2)^2}{(1+|u|^2)^{(d+5)/2}}\dd u.
\]
Write \(A=1+|u|^2\).  The odd term in the expansion of
\((A+|z|^2+2u\cdot z)^2\) integrates to zero, and rotational invariance
gives
\[
 \int(u\cdot z)^2(1+|u|^2)^{-(d+5)/2}\dd u
 =\frac{|z|^2}{d}\int |u|^2(1+|u|^2)^{-(d+5)/2}\dd u.
\]
The three normalized beta integrals needed here are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 c_d\int(1+|u|^2)^{-(d+1)/2}\dd u&=1,\\
 c_d\int(1+|u|^2)^{-(d+3)/2}\dd u&=\frac1{d+1},\\
 c_d\int(1+|u|^2)^{-(d+5)/2}\dd u
 &=\frac3{(d+1)(d+3)}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Substitution proves \eqref{eq:critical-lq-exact-translation-norm}.

For \(|z|\le1\), the local quotient--Taylor estimate
\eqref{eq:local-multidim-taylor-remainder} implies the first line of
\eqref{eq:critical-lq-global-remainder}.  For \(|z|>1\), the exact identity
gives \(\|F_\cdot(z)\|_{q_d}\le C_d|z|^{4/q_d}=C_d|z|^{p_d}\).
Every coefficient of \(T_m\) is bounded in \(y\), and \(m\le p_d\), so
\(\|T_m(\cdot,z)\|_{q_d}\le C_d|z|^{p_d}\).  Finally,
\(m+1>p_d\), which proves the last inequality for \(|z|\le1\).
\end{proof}

For \(0<\alpha<2\), let \(p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\) be the density of any
centred isotropic strictly \(\alpha\)-stable law on \(\RR^d\), and use the
spatial-scale normalization
\[
 p_s^{(\alpha,d)}(x)=s^{-d}p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(x/s),\qquad s>0.
\]
Changing the scale parameter in the characteristic exponent only changes
the choice of \(p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\), so this notation covers every isotropic
strictly stable kernel.  Put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-critical-exponents}
 \beta=d+\alpha,\qquad
 q_{\alpha,d}:=\min\left\{2,1+\frac4\beta\right\},\qquad
 p_{\alpha,d}:=\frac4{q_{\alpha,d}}
 =\max\left\{2,\frac{4(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+4}\right\}.
\end{equation}
Write \(\Omega_{\alpha,d}(\dd y)=p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)\dd y\) and
\[
F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)
:=\frac{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y-z)}{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}.
\]

\begin{proposition}[Stable-kernel input package]
\label{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}
Put \(\beta=d+\alpha\).  For every multi-index \(\gamma\), there are positive
constants \(c,C,C_\gamma\), depending on \(d,\alpha\) and the chosen stable
scale, such that
\begin{align}
 c(1+|y|)^{-\beta}&\le p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)
 \le C(1+|y|)^{-\beta},\label{eq:stable-input-density}\\
 |\partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)|
 &\le C_\gamma(1+|y|)^{-\beta-|\gamma|},\label{eq:stable-input-derivative}\\
 \frac{|\partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)|}
 {p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}
 &\le C_\gamma(1+|y|)^{-|\gamma|}.
 \label{eq:stable-input-derivative-quotient}
\end{align}
In particular, \(p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\) is strictly positive and smooth,
\(\|\nabla\log p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\|_\infty<\infty\), and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-input-translation-continuity}
 \|\partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(\mathord\cdot-z)
       -\partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\|_1\longrightarrow0
 \qquad(z\to0).
\end{equation}
If the characteristic exponent is changed from \(|\xi|^\alpha\) to
\(a|\xi|^\alpha\), put \(\lambda=a^{1/\alpha}\).  The new unit-scale density
is \(p_{1,a}(y)=\lambda^{-d}p_1(y/\lambda)\).  Thus the density bound has
factor \(\lambda^{-d}\), the derivative bound has factor
\(\lambda^{-d-|\gamma|}\), and the quotient bound has factor
\(\lambda^{-|\gamma|}\), with \(1+|y|\) replaced throughout by
\(1+|y|/\lambda\).  Equivalently, all later
constants are locally uniform when \(a\) ranges in a compact subset of
\((0,\infty)\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Properties (G)(i)--(iii) of \cite{IshigeKawakamiMichihisa2017}, also recorded
in the refined formulation of
\cite{IshigeKawakamiMichihisa2022RefinedFractional}, give strict positivity,
smoothness, the derivative upper bounds, and the positive tail asymptotic
\(p_1(y)\asymp |y|^{-d-\alpha}\) outside a sufficiently large ball.  The
tail asymptotic supplies the lower bound in
\eqref{eq:stable-input-density} there.  On the remaining compact ball,
strict positivity and continuity give a positive minimum; enlarging the
upper constant completes the global two-sided density bound.  Dividing
\eqref{eq:stable-input-derivative} by this lower bound proves
\eqref{eq:stable-input-derivative-quotient}, including the log-gradient
bound.  The derivative estimate makes every \(\partial^\gamma p_1\)
integrable, so ordinary \(L^1\)-translation continuity gives
\eqref{eq:stable-input-translation-continuity}.  The assertions about \(a\)
follow directly by differentiating the displayed dilation formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Stable critical translation remainder]
\label{lem:stable-critical-translation-remainder}
Let \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), \(p=p_{\alpha,d}\),
\(q=q_{\alpha,d}\), and \(m=\lfloor p\rfloor\).  If
\(T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(y,z)\) is the Taylor polynomial of
\(F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\) at \(z=0\) through degree \(m\), then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-translation-lq-growth}
 c_{\alpha,d,q}(1+|z|)^{\beta(q-1)}
 \le \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}^q
 \le C_{\alpha,d,q}(1+|z|)^{\beta(q-1)}.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-critical-global-remainder}
 \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,z)\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}
 \le C_{\alpha,d}
 \begin{cases}
  |z|^{m+1},&|z|\le1,\\
  |z|^p,&|z|>1,
 \end{cases}
 \le C_{\alpha,d}|z|^p.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package} supplies all density,
derivative, quotient, and translation estimates used below.  The upper
bound in \eqref{eq:stable-translation-lq-growth} follows from
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \int p_1(y-z)^q p_1(y)^{1-q}\dd y
 &\le C\int(1+|y-z|)^{-\beta q}
              (1+|y|)^{\beta(q-1)}\dd y\\
 &\le C(1+|z|)^{\beta(q-1)}
       \int(1+|y-z|)^{-\beta}\dd y,
 \end{aligned}
\]
where \(p_1=p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\) and
\(1+|y|\le(1+|z|)(1+|y-z|)\).  The final integral is finite because
\(\beta>d\).  For the lower bound, integrate over \(|y-z|\le1\) and use
\eqref{eq:stable-input-density}; this gives the claimed power
for \(|z|\ge2\).  Positivity and continuity on bounded \(z\)-sets complete
the estimate.

For \(|z|\le1\), Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package} also gives
\(p_1(y-\theta z)\le C p_1(y)\), uniformly in \(0\le\theta\le1\).
Taylor's formula along the segment from \(y\) to \(y-z\), followed by the
derivative bound in \eqref{eq:stable-input-derivative}, therefore
gives the pointwise bound
\(|F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(y,z)|\le C|z|^{m+1}\), uniformly
in \(y\).  For \(|z|>1\), \eqref{eq:stable-translation-lq-growth} gives
\(\|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\|_q\le C|z|^{\beta(1-1/q)}\).  The Taylor
coefficients are bounded, so
\(\|T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,z)\|_q\le C|z|^m\).  Finally,
\[
 \beta(1-1/q)\le p,\qquad m\le p<m+1,
\]
with equality in the first relation when \(\beta>4\).  These observations
prove \eqref{eq:stable-critical-global-remainder}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Critical Bregman perturbation bound]
\label{lem:critical-lq-kl-perturbation}
Let \(1<q\le2\) and
\(\Phi(s)=(1+s)\log(1+s)-s\) on \([-1,\infty)\), with
\(0\log0=0\).  There is a constant \(C_q\) such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-bregman-pointwise-bound}
 0\le \Phi(u+v)-\Phi(u)-\log(1+u)v\le C_q|v|^q
\end{equation}
whenever \(|u|\le1/4\) and \(u+v\ge-1\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The lower bound is convexity.  If \(|v|\le1/2\), the segment between
\(u\) and \(u+v\) is contained in \([-3/4,3/4]\).  Since
\(\Phi''(s)=(1+s)^{-1}\) there, Taylor's theorem gives an upper bound
\(C v^2\le C|v|^q\).  If \(v<-1/2\), the admissible pairs
\((u,v)\) range over a compact set and \(|v|^q\ge2^{-q}\); continuity at
\(u+v=-1\) gives the result.  If \(v>1/2\), direct expansion of the left
side shows that it is at most \(C(1+v)\log(1+v)+Cv\), which is bounded by
\(C_qv^q\).  These three regions prove
\eqref{eq:critical-bregman-pointwise-bound}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Optimal uniform sufficient moment exponent for stable KL asymptotics]
\label{thm:high-dimensional-kl-moment-threshold}
Let \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), and let \(\nu\) be a probability law on
\(\RR^d\) with mean \(\bar\gamma\).  Put
\(X=\gamma-\bar\gamma\), and assume
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-kl-moment-hypothesis}
 \EE|X|^{p_{\alpha,d}}<\infty,
 \qquad
 p_{\alpha,d}=\max\left\{2,
 \frac{4(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+4}\right\},
\end{equation}
then the covariance \(\Sigma=\EE[XX^{\mathsf T}]\) is finite and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-kl-leading-asymptotic}
 H_{\alpha,d}(s):=
 D_{\rm KL}\!\left(p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu\,\middle\|\,
 p_s^{(\alpha,d)}(\mathord\cdot-\bar\gamma)\right)
 =\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)s^{-4}+o(s^{-4}),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-leading-covariance-functional}
 b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}(y)
 :=\frac1{2p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}
   \sum_{i,j=1}^d\Sigma_{ij}\partial_{ij}p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y),
 \qquad
 \mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)
 :=\frac12\int b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}^2\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}.
\end{equation}
The exponent is optimal only in the following uniform sense.  For every
\(0<r<2\), there is a mean-zero law with finite \(r\)th absolute moment
and \(\limsup_{s\to\infty}s^4H_{\alpha,d}(s)=+\infty\).  If
\(d+\alpha>4\), then for every \(2\le r<p_{\alpha,d}\) the counterexample
may additionally be chosen with positive-definite finite covariance.
Thus no smaller moment exponent implies
\eqref{eq:critical-kl-leading-asymptotic} uniformly over its entire moment
class, and the endpoint belongs to the sufficient side.

This is not a law-by-law moment criterion.  When \(d+\alpha>4\), finite
\(p_{\alpha,d}\)-moment is not asserted to be necessary for an individual
law; the exact finite-covariance criterion is the nonlinear raw-tail energy
in Theorem~\ref{thm:stable-law-by-law-decomposition} below.  When
\(d+\alpha\le4\), the exponent is two and boundedness of
\(s^4H_{\alpha,d}(s)\) does force finite covariance, as the proof below
shows.  For \(\alpha=1\) with the standard normalization
\(p_1^{(1,d)}=P_1^{(d)}\), one has
\(\mathcal Q_{1,d}=\mathcal Q_d\), so the theorem contains the radial
Poisson result above.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Translation permits us to assume \(\bar\gamma=0\).  Fix
\(q=q_{\alpha,d}\), \(p=p_{\alpha,d}\), and \(m=\lfloor p\rfloor\),
and write
\[
 R_m(y,z)=F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(y,z),
 \qquad r_s(y)=\EE R_m(y,X/s).
\]
Minkowski's inequality and
\eqref{eq:stable-critical-global-remainder} give
\[
 s^p\|R_m(\cdot,X/s)\|_q\le C_{\alpha,d}|X|^p.
\]
For each fixed \(X\), the local part of the same estimate and \(m+1>p\)
give
\[
 s^p\|R_m(\cdot,X/s)\|_q
 \le C_{\alpha,d}|X|^{m+1}s^{p-m-1}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Dominated convergence therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-lq-integrated-remainder}
 \|r_s\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}=o(s^{-p}).
\end{equation}

Centering removes the linear Taylor layer.  Averaging the remaining layers
gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-kl-quotient-decomposition}
 \delta_s^{(\alpha,d)}=u_s+r_s,
 \qquad
 u_s=s^{-2}b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}
       +\mathbf 1_{\{m=3\}}s^{-3}B_3,
\end{equation}
where \(B_3\) is a bounded linear combination of third-order modes.  In the
second case the required third moments exist because \(p\ge3\).  Hence
\(\|u_s\|_\infty=O(s^{-2})\).  The boundedness of all these modes follows
from Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}.

The identity
\(F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\Omega_{\alpha,d}(\dd y)
=p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y-z)\dd y\) shows that every translated quotient has
integral one.  Moreover,
\(\int|F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-1|\Omega_{\alpha,d}(\dd y)\le2\), so Tonelli's
theorem gives \(\delta_s^{(\alpha,d)}\in L^1(\Omega_{\alpha,d})\) with
zero integral.  The KL change of variables is therefore
\[
 H_{\alpha,d}(s)=\int\Phi(\delta_s^{(\alpha,d)})\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
\]
in the extended sense.  For all sufficiently large \(s\), apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:critical-lq-kl-perturbation} to \(u=u_s\), \(v=r_s\).
HÃ¶lder's inequality and \eqref{eq:critical-lq-integrated-remainder} give
\begin{align*}
 \left|H_{\alpha,d}(s)-\int\Phi(u_s)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}\right|
 &\le \|\log(1+u_s)\|_{q/(q-1)}\|r_s\|_q
       +C_q\|r_s\|_q^q\\
 &\le O(s^{-2})o(s^{-p})+o(s^{-pq})=o(s^{-4}),
\end{align*}
because \(p\ge2\) and \(pq=4\).
This estimate also proves that the extended KL integral is finite for all
sufficiently large \(s\).

Finally, the boundedness of the retained modes permits a uniform Taylor
expansion of \(\Phi(u_s)\).  From
\eqref{eq:critical-kl-quotient-decomposition},
\[
 \int\Phi(u_s)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
 =\frac{s^{-4}}2\int b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}^2\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
   +o(s^{-4})
 =\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)s^{-4}+o(s^{-4}),
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:critical-kl-leading-asymptotic}.

We first prove the obstruction below two moments.  If
\(\limsup_{s\to\infty}s^4H_{\alpha,d}(s)<\infty\), Pinsker's inequality
and scaling give, for every fixed \(\xi\in\RR^d\),
\[
 |\widehat p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(\xi)|
 |\varphi_X(\xi/s)-1|
 \le \|p_1^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu_s-p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\|_1
 \le \sqrt{2H_{\alpha,d}(s)}=O(s^{-2}),
\]
where \(\nu_s\) is the law of \(X/s\).  Since the stable characteristic
function never vanishes, take \(\xi=e\) for a unit vector \(e\), multiply
the real part by \(s^2\), and use Fatou's lemma to obtain
\[
 \frac12\EE(e\cdot X)^2
 \le \liminf_{s\to\infty}s^2
       \EE[1-\cos((e\cdot X)/s)]<\infty.
\]
Thus bounded scaled entropy forces finite covariance.  Given \(0<r<2\),
choose \(a\in(\max\{1,r\},2)\) and put symmetric masses proportional to
\(n^{-a-1}\) at \(\pm ne_1\), with the remaining mass at zero.  This law
has mean zero and finite \(r\)th moment but infinite variance, so its scaled
entropy has infinite limsup.

It remains to prove optimality between two and \(p\) when \(\beta>4\).
Fix \(2\le r<p\), choose positive \(a_j\) with \(\sum_ja_j<\infty\), and
put symmetric masses \(w_j/2\) at \(\pm R_je_1\), where
\(w_j=a_jR_j^{-r}\).  Add a sufficiently small bounded symmetric spanning
component.  The resulting law has positive-definite finite covariance and
finite \(r\)th moment.  Set
\[
 s_j=\kappa R_jw_j^{1/\beta},\qquad
 A_j=B(R_je_1,s_j).
\]
The component at \(R_je_1\) gives
\((p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu)(A_j)\ge c_{\alpha,d}w_j\).  On the other hand,
\eqref{eq:stable-input-density} and \(s_j/R_j\to0\) give
\[
 p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}(A_j)
 \le C_{\alpha,d}(s_j/R_j)^\beta
 =C_{\alpha,d}\kappa^\beta w_j.
\]
Choose \(\kappa\) so that
\(C_{\alpha,d}\kappa^\beta<c_{\alpha,d}\).  Data processing to
\(\{A_j,A_j^c\}\) and
Lemma~\ref{lem:bernoulli-kl-linear-separation} then yield
\(H_{\alpha,d}(s_j)\ge c w_j\), and hence
\[
 s_j^4H_{\alpha,d}(s_j)
 \ge cR_j^4w_j^{1+4/\beta}
 =ca_j^{q_{\alpha,d}}R_j^{4-rq_{\alpha,d}}.
\]
Here \(q_{\alpha,d}=1+4/\beta\) and
\(r<p=4/q_{\alpha,d}\), so the exponent of \(R_j\) is positive.
Recursive choice of the radii makes \(s_j\to\infty\) and the last display
unbounded while preserving all moment assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[All-order stable critical remainder]
\label{lem:all-order-stable-critical-remainder}
Let \(r\ge1\), put \(\beta=d+\alpha\), and define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-critical-exponents}
 q_{r,\alpha,d}:=\min\left\{2,1+\frac{2r}{d+\alpha}\right\},
 \qquad
 p_{r,\alpha,d}:=\frac{2r}{q_{r,\alpha,d}}
 =\max\left\{r,\frac{2r(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+2r}\right\}.
\end{equation}
Let \(q=q_{r,\alpha,d}\), \(p=p_{r,\alpha,d}\), and
\(m=\lfloor p\rfloor\).  If \(T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(y,z)\) is the Taylor
polynomial of \(F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\) at zero through degree \(m\), then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-critical-remainder}
 \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,z)\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}
 \le C_{\alpha,d,r}
 \begin{cases}
  |z|^{m+1},&|z|\le1,\\
  |z|^p,&|z|>1,
 \end{cases}
 \le C_{\alpha,d,r}|z|^p.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if a probability law \(\lambda\) on \(\RR^d\) has finite
\(p\)th absolute moment and
\[
 q_s^\lambda(y):=\int F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(x/s)\lambda(\dd x),
\]
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-integrated-remainder}
 q_s^\lambda
 =1+\sum_{j=1}^m s^{-j}B_j^\lambda+r_s^\lambda,
 \qquad
 \|r_s^\lambda\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}=o(s^{-p}),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-moment-modes}
 B_j^\lambda(y):=
 \frac{(-1)^j}{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}
 \sum_{|\gamma|=j}\frac{m_\gamma(\lambda)}{\gamma!}
 \partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y),
 \qquad
 m_\gamma(\lambda):=\int x^\gamma\lambda(\dd x).
\end{equation}
Every \(B_j^\lambda\) in this display is bounded.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The proof of \eqref{eq:stable-translation-lq-growth} applies verbatim for
every fixed \(1<q\le2\) and gives
\[
 \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}
 \le C(1+|z|)^{\beta(1-1/q)}.
\]
The local Taylor argument in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:stable-critical-translation-remainder} gives the first line
of \eqref{eq:all-order-stable-critical-remainder}.  For \(|z|>1\), the
Taylor modes are bounded by
Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}, and
hence
\[
 \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,z)\|_q
 \le C\{|z|^{\beta(1-1/q)}+|z|^m\}\le C|z|^p.
\]
Indeed, \(m\le p\), while
\(\beta(1-1/q)\le p\); in the non-Hilbert regime
\(\beta>2r\), both sides of the latter inequality equal
\(2r\beta/(\beta+2r)\).  Since \(m+1>p\), the final inequality in
\eqref{eq:all-order-stable-critical-remainder} also holds on the unit ball.

Taylor's formula gives \eqref{eq:all-order-stable-integrated-remainder}
before its norm assertion.  For fixed \(x\), the local estimate implies
\[
 s^p\|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(x/s)
       -T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,x/s)\|_q\longrightarrow0,
\]
whereas \eqref{eq:all-order-stable-critical-remainder} bounds this expression
by \(C|x|^p\).  Minkowski's inequality and dominated convergence prove the
claimed \(L^q\) remainder.  Boundedness of the modes follows again from
Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Two-background critical Bregman transfer]
\label{lem:two-background-critical-bregman-transfer}
Let \(1<q\le2\), \(p\ge r>0\), and \(pq=2r\).  On a probability space
\((E,\Omega)\), suppose \(g_s\ge c_s>0\),
\[
 \int g_s\dd\Omega=1,\qquad c_s\longrightarrow1,
 \qquad \|g_s-1\|_{L^1(\Omega)}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Let \(B\in L^\infty(\Omega)\), and suppose
\[
 v_s=s^{-r}B+o(s^{-r})\quad\hbox{in }L^\infty(\Omega),
 \qquad \|e_s\|_{L^q(\Omega)}=o(s^{-p}).
\]
If \(g_s+v_s+e_s\ge0\) and both \(g_s\Omega\) and
\((g_s+v_s+e_s)\Omega\) are probability measures, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-background-critical-bregman-transfer}
 D_{\rm KL}((g_s+v_s+e_s)\Omega\|g_s\Omega)
 =\frac{s^{-2r}}2\int B^2\dd\Omega+o(s^{-2r}).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

The hypotheses on the denominator in this lemma deliberately stop short of
\(L^\infty\)-convergence to one.  They require only a positive lower bound
approaching one, mass normalization, and \(L^1\)-convergence.  This weaker
interface is what permits a heavy-tailed translated mixture to serve as the
background.

\begin{proof}
For \(g>0\), write \(\Psi_g(z)=g\Phi(z/g)\).  Scaling
Lemma~\ref{lem:critical-lq-kl-perturbation} shows, whenever
\(|v/g|\le1/4\) and \(g+v+e\ge0\), that
\[
 0\le\Psi_g(v+e)-\Psi_g(v)
      -\log(1+v/g)e\le C_q g^{1-q}|e|^q.
\]
For large \(s\), the hypotheses give \(g_s\ge1/2\) and
\(\|v_s/g_s\|_\infty\le1/4\).  Therefore H\"older's inequality yields
\begin{align*}
 &\left|D_{\rm KL}((g_s+v_s+e_s)\Omega\|g_s\Omega)
       -\int\Psi_{g_s}(v_s)\dd\Omega\right|\\
 &\qquad\le
 C\|v_s\|_{L^{q/(q-1)}}\|e_s\|_{L^q}
 +C\|e_s\|_{L^q}^q
 =o(s^{-r-p})+o(s^{-pq})=o(s^{-2r}).
\end{align*}
Uniform Taylor expansion at zero gives
\[
 \int\Psi_{g_s}(v_s)\dd\Omega
 =\frac12\int\frac{v_s^2}{g_s}\dd\Omega+O(\|v_s\|_\infty^3).
\]
Finally,
\[
 \left|\int B^2(g_s^{-1}-1)\dd\Omega\right|
 \le2\|B\|_\infty^2\|g_s-1\|_1\longrightarrow0,
\]
and \eqref{eq:two-background-critical-bregman-transfer} follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite-difference moment blocks]
\label{lem:stable-finite-difference-blocks}
Let \(r\ge1\), let \(e\) be a unit vector, and define
\[
 \sigma_R:=2^{1-r}\sum_{k=0}^r(-1)^{r-k}\binom rk
                 \delta_{(k+1)Re}=A_R^+-A_R^-.
\]
Then \(A_R^+\) and \(A_R^-\) are probability measures and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-block-moment-identities}
 \int x^\gamma\dd\sigma_R(x)=0\quad(|\gamma|<r),
 \qquad
 \int(e\cdot x)^r\dd\sigma_R(x)=2^{1-r}r!R^r.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The positive and negative binomial coefficients each sum to \(2^{r-1}\),
and the order-\(r\) forward-difference identity gives
\eqref{eq:stable-block-moment-identities}.  In particular, when \(r=1\),
\(\sigma_R=\delta_{2Re}-\delta_{Re}\); the same cancellation and nonzero
first-difference conclusions hold without a separate construction.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Moving-ball probability separation]
\label{lem:stable-moving-ball-probability-separation}
Let \(\beta=d+\alpha\), let \(A_R^\pm\) be the blocks in
Lemma~\ref{lem:stable-finite-difference-blocks}, and suppose
\[
 R_{j+1}>4(r+1)R_j,
 \qquad w_j>0,
 \qquad \sum_jw_j<1.
\]
Define
\[
 \nu=\left(1-\sum_jw_j\right)\delta_0+\sum_jw_jA_{R_j}^+,
 \qquad
 \eta=\left(1-\sum_jw_j\right)\delta_0+\sum_jw_jA_{R_j}^-.
\]
Put \(x_j=(r+1)R_je\), choose
\(s_j=\kappa R_jw_j^{1/\beta}<R_j/4\), and set
\(E_j=B(x_j,s_j)\).  There are constants \(a_r>0\) and
\(C_{\alpha,d,r}<\infty\), independent of \(j,\kappa,R_j,w_j\), such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-moving-ball-probability-separation}
 (p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu)(E_j)\ge a_rw_j,
 \qquad
 (p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\eta)(E_j)
 \le C_{\alpha,d,r}\kappa^\beta w_j.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The endpoint coefficient in \(A_{R_j}^+\) at \(x_j\) is \(2^{1-r}\).
Stable scaling and positivity therefore give
\[
 (p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu)(E_j)
 \ge 2^{1-r}w_j\int_{B(0,1)}p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)\dd y
 =:a_rw_j.
\]
We verify the separation from every atom of \(\eta\).  In block \(j\),
opposite-sign atoms are at least \(R_j\) from \(x_j\).  Every earlier atom
has norm at most \((r+1)R_{j-1}<R_j/4\), whereas every later atom has norm at
least \(R_{j+1}>4(r+1)R_j\); the atom at zero obeys the earlier-atom bound.
After subtracting the radius \(s_j<R_j/4\), every such atom \(z\) satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-moving-ball-distance}
 \operatorname{dist}(z,E_j)\ge3R_j/4.
\end{equation}
For \(y\in E_j\), the stable density upper bound and scaling now give
\[
 p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}(y-z)
 \le C_{\alpha,d,r}s_j^\alpha R_j^{-\beta}.
\]

Integrating over the ball and summing against all probability weights of
\(\eta\) yields
\[

 =C_{\alpha,d,r}\kappa^\beta w_j,
\]
which is the second assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform Bernoulli relative-entropy separation]
\label{lem:bernoulli-kl-linear-separation}
Let \(0<b<a\).  If \(u\ge aw\) and \(v\le bw\) are Bernoulli parameters,
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bernoulli-kl-linear-separation}
 D_{\rm KL}(\operatorname{Ber}(u)\|\operatorname{Ber}(v))
 \ge a\left\{\log\frac ab-1+\frac ba\right\}w.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If \(v=0<u\), the relative entropy is infinite.  Otherwise \(u>v>0\), and
\[
 (1-u)\log\frac{1-u}{1-v}\ge-(u-v).
\]
Writing \(\theta=v/u\le b/a<1\) therefore gives
\[
 D_{\rm KL}(\operatorname{Ber}(u)\|\operatorname{Ber}(v))
 \ge u\{\log(1/\theta)-1+\theta\}
 \ge aw\left\{\log\frac ab-1+\frac ba\right\},
\]
because the braced function is decreasing on \((0,1)\).
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Gaussian benchmark and priority.}
Let \(\rho_t(x)=(2\pi t)^{-d/2}e^{-|x|^2/(2t)}\).  Under a finite
exponential square moment for each centred input, Chen and Niles-Weed
\cite[Theorem~2.5]{ChenNilesWeed2022SmoothedWasserstein} prove that moment
matching below order \(r=n+1\), followed by a nonzero difference at order
\(r\), implies, with
\(\Delta m_\gamma=m_\gamma(\mu)-m_\gamma(\eta)\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:chen-niles-weed-gaussian-kl-benchmark}
 \lim_{t\to\infty}t^rD_{\rm KL}(\mu*\rho_t\|\eta*\rho_t)
 =\frac12\sum_{|\gamma|=r}\frac{|\Delta m_\gamma|^2}{\gamma!}.
\end{equation}
Putting \(s=\sqrt t\) gives the same \(s^{-2r}\) scaling as below.  For the
standard Gaussian \(g=\rho_1\), the identities
\((-1)^{|\gamma|}\partial^\gamma g=H_\gamma g\) and
\(\int H_\gamma H_\delta g=\gamma!\mathbf1_{\gamma=\delta}\) identify the
right side of \eqref{eq:chen-niles-weed-gaussian-kl-benchmark} exactly with
the quadratic functional \eqref{eq:all-order-stable-leading-functional} at
the Gaussian boundary \(\alpha=2\).  Accordingly, the first-unmatched
quadratic KL mechanism and its positivity are prior work in the Gaussian
case.  The theorem below contributes the heavy-tailed range \(0<\alpha<2\),
the critical complete-moment exponent, endpoint sufficiency, and uniform
sharpness over those moment classes.

\begin{theorem}[All-order first unmatched tensor under stable smoothing]
\label{thm:all-order-stable-first-unmatched-moment}
Let \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), and let \(r\ge1\) be an integer.  Define
\(q_{r,\alpha,d}\) and \(p_{r,\alpha,d}\) by
\eqref{eq:all-order-stable-critical-exponents}.  Let \(\nu,\eta\) be
probability laws on \(\RR^d\) such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-moment-hypotheses}
 m_\gamma(\nu)=m_\gamma(\eta)\quad(|\gamma|<r),
 \qquad
 \int|x|^{p_{r,\alpha,d}}(\nu+\eta)(\dd x)<\infty.
\end{equation}
Put
\[
 \Delta_r:=\int_{\RR^d}x^{\otimes r}(\nu-\eta)(\dd x)
 \in\operatorname{Sym}^r(\RR^d),
\]
so its multi-index coordinates are
\(\Delta m_\gamma=m_\gamma(\nu)-m_\gamma(\eta)\), and suppose
\(\Delta_r\ne0\).  With the Euclidean contraction of symmetric tensors,
define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-leading-mode}
 B_{\Delta_r}(y):=
 \frac{(-1)^r}{r!p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}
 \langle\Delta_r,D^rp_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)\rangle
 =\frac{(-1)^r}{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}
 \sum_{|\gamma|=r}\frac{\Delta m_\gamma}{\gamma!}
 \partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-leading-functional}
 \mathcal Q_{\alpha,d,r}(\Delta_r)
 :=\frac12\int_{\RR^d}B_{\Delta_r}(y)^2
                  \Omega_{\alpha,d}(\dd y).
\end{equation}
Then \(\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d,r}(\Delta_r)>0\), the quadratic form is
invariant under \(\Delta_r\mapsto U^{\otimes r}\Delta_r\) for every
\(U\in O(d)\), and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-first-unmatched-asymptotic}
 D_{\rm KL}(p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu\|p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\eta)
 =\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d,r}(\Delta_r)s^{-2r}+o(s^{-2r}).
\end{equation}

The exponent \(p_{r,\alpha,d}\) is optimal as a uniform sufficient
absolute-moment hypothesis, with its endpoint included.  More precisely,
if \(d+\alpha>2r\), then for every
\(r\le\rho<p_{r,\alpha,d}\) there are probability laws \(\nu,\eta\)
having finite \(\rho\)th absolute moments, matching every tensor moment
below order \(r\), and having a finite nonzero order-\(r\) tensor difference,
but
\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-sharpness}
 \limsup_{s\to\infty}s^{2r}
 D_{\rm KL}(p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu\|p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\eta)=+\infty.
\end{equation}
For \(0<\rho<r\), finiteness of the \(\rho\)th absolute moment does not
even guarantee that the tensor in \eqref{eq:all-order-stable-leading-mode}
is defined throughout the moment class.  Thus the latter observation is a
domain obstruction, whereas \eqref{eq:all-order-stable-sharpness} is the
analytic sharpness statement on laws for which the leading tensor exists.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write \(q=q_{r,\alpha,d}\), \(p=p_{r,\alpha,d}\), and
\(m=\lfloor p\rfloor\).  Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:all-order-stable-critical-remainder} to both laws.  Their
common moments below order \(r\) cancel, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-two-quotient-split}
 q_s^\nu-q_s^\eta=v_s+e_s,
 \quad
 v_s=\sum_{j=r}^m s^{-j}(B_j^\nu-B_j^\eta),
 \quad
 e_s=r_s^\nu-r_s^\eta.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\[
 s^rv_s\longrightarrow B_{\Delta_r}\quad\hbox{in }L^\infty,
 \qquad \|e_s\|_q=o(s^{-p}).
\]
The intermediate modes \(r<j\le m\) in
\eqref{eq:all-order-stable-two-quotient-split} are essential: unless their
moments also match, they are not part of the \(o(s^{-p})\) remainder.

No part of this argument requires \(r\ge2\).  At \(r=1\), the endpoint
formula still gives \(p\ge1\), hence the assumed \(p\)-moment supplies the
first moments and \(\EE|X|<\infty\); also \(m+1>p\) and \(pq=2\).  Thus the
critical remainder and the two-background transfer have exactly the powers
needed for an \(o(s^{-2})\) error.  Lemma~\ref{lem:stable-finite-difference-blocks}
records the corresponding first-difference block used for sharpness.

Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package} implies
\(\|\nabla\log p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\|_\infty\le L_{\alpha,d}\).  Hence, if
\(X\) has law \(\lambda\),
\[
 q_s^\lambda(y)
 \ge\EE\exp(-L_{\alpha,d}|X|/s)
 \ge\exp(-L_{\alpha,d}\EE|X|/s),
\]
uniformly in \(y\).  The last expression tends to one.  Translation
continuity of \(p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\) in \(L^1\) gives, by Tonelli and dominated
convergence,
\[
 \|q_s^\eta-1\|_{L^1(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}
 \le\int\|p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(\mathord\cdot-x/s)
              -p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\|_1\,\eta(\dd x)\longrightarrow0;
\]
the integrand is bounded by two.  A second Tonelli calculation gives
\(\int q_s^\lambda\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}=1\) for every probability law
\(\lambda\).  These are precisely the positive lower bound, mass
normalization, and \(L^1\)-convergence required of the denominator by
Lemma~\ref{lem:two-background-critical-bregman-transfer}; no
\(L^\infty\)-convergence of \(q_s^\eta\) to one is used.  Taking
\(g_s=q_s^\eta\) in that lemma proves
\eqref{eq:all-order-stable-first-unmatched-asymptotic}.

Boundedness of \(B_{\Delta_r}\) makes
\(\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d,r}\) finite.  If it were zero, then
\[
 \sum_{|\gamma|=r}\frac{\Delta m_\gamma}{\gamma!}
 \partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}=0
\]
almost everywhere.  Fourier transformation in the sense of tempered
distributions gives a homogeneous polynomial in \(\xi\), with coefficients
\(\Delta m_\gamma/\gamma!\), multiplied by the nowhere-vanishing stable
characteristic function.  The polynomial must vanish identically, contrary
to \(\Delta_r\ne0\).  This proves strict positivity.  If \(U\in O(d)\),
isotropy and the tensor chain rule give
\(B_{U^{\otimes r}\Delta_r}(Uy)=B_{\Delta_r}(y)\).  Orthogonal invariance of
\(\Omega_{\alpha,d}\) then proves the asserted invariance of \(\mathcal Q\).
For \(d\ge2\), under the homogeneous-polynomial identification, the standard
trace/harmonic decomposition
\[
 \operatorname{Sym}^r(\RR^d)
 =\bigoplus_{k=0}^{\lfloor r/2\rfloor}
   |x|^{2k}\mathcal H_{r-2k}
\]
is multiplicity-free under \(O(d)\).  Hence the self-adjoint operator of
\(\mathcal Q\) is scalar on each harmonic summand; the positivity just proved
shows that all these scalars are strictly positive.  No formula for the
individual scalars is needed below.

It remains to establish sharpness.  Assume \(\beta=d+\alpha>2r\), so
\[
 q=1+\frac{2r}{\beta},\qquad p=\frac{2r}{q}>r.
\]
Fix a unit vector \(e\), and let \(A_R^\pm\) be the probability blocks from
Lemma~\ref{lem:stable-finite-difference-blocks}.

Choose \(a_j>0\) with \(\sum_ja_j<\infty\).  Choose the radii recursively so
that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-separated-block-radii}
 R_{j+1}>4(r+1)R_j,
\end{equation}
and enlarge each new radius further whenever necessary below.  Put
\(w_j=a_jR_j^{-\rho}\), with \(\sum_jw_j<1\), and define
\[
 \nu=\left(1-\sum_jw_j\right)\delta_0+\sum_jw_jA_{R_j}^+,
 \qquad
 \eta=\left(1-\sum_jw_j\right)\delta_0+\sum_jw_jA_{R_j}^-.
\]
They have finite \(\rho\)th moments.  Since \(\rho\ge r\),
\eqref{eq:stable-block-moment-identities} also shows that their
order-\(r\) tensor difference is finite and nonzero.

The endpoint \(x_j=(r+1)R_je\) belongs to \(A_{R_j}^+\) and not to
\(A_{R_j}^-\).  Let \(E_j\) be the ball of radius
\[
 s_j=\kappa R_jw_j^{1/\beta}
\]
about \(x_j\).  Recursive enlargement of \(R_j\) makes \(s_j\to\infty\);
also \(s_j/R_j=\kappa w_j^{1/\beta}<1/4\) for all sufficiently large \(j\).
Lemma~\ref{lem:stable-moving-ball-probability-separation} gives both
probability bounds, after explicitly separating \(E_j\) from every
opposite-sign atom in the same, preceding, and succeeding blocks.
Choose \(\kappa\) so that
\(C_{\alpha,d,r}\kappa^\beta<a_r\).  Data processing to
\(\{E_j,E_j^c\}\), followed by
Lemma~\ref{lem:bernoulli-kl-linear-separation}, gives
\[
 D_{\rm KL}(p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu\|
            p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\eta)\ge c w_j.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 s_j^{2r}D_{\rm KL}(p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu\|
                    p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\eta)
 \ge cR_j^{2r}w_j^{1+2r/\beta}
 =ca_j^qR_j^{2r-\rho q}.
\]
The final exponent is positive exactly when \(\rho<p=2r/q\).
Recursive enlargement of \(R_j\) proves
\eqref{eq:all-order-stable-sharpness}.  Finally, for \(\rho<r\), a
one-dimensional Pareto law supported on the \(e\)-axis may have finite
\(\rho\)th and infinite \(r\)th absolute moment, proving the stated domain
obstruction.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Stable Gaussian-quadrature entropy threshold]
\label{cor:stable-gaussian-quadrature-threshold}
Let \(0<\alpha<2\), \(n\ge1\), and let \(\nu\) be a probability law on
\(\RR\) such that
\[
 \EE|X|^{2n-1}<\infty,\qquad |\operatorname{supp}\nu|\ge n.
\]
Let \(G_n\nu\) and \(\pi_n\) be its \(n\)-node Gaussian quadrature law and
monic degree-\(n\) orthogonal polynomial, respectively.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-gaussian-quadrature-finite}
 \EE|X|^{2n}<\infty
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \lim_{s\to\infty}s^{4n}
 D_{\rm KL}(p_s^{(\alpha,1)}*\nu\|
            p_s^{(\alpha,1)}*G_n\nu)
 =C_{\alpha,n}\|\pi_n\|_{L^2(\nu)}^4,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-gaussian-quadrature-constant}
 C_{\alpha,n}:=
 \frac1{2((2n)!)^2}\int_{\RR}
 \frac{(\partial^{2n}p_1^{(\alpha,1)}(y))^2}
      {p_1^{(\alpha,1)}(y)}\dd y>0.
\end{equation}
On the other hand,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-gaussian-quadrature-infinite}
 \EE|X|^{2n}=\infty
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 s^{4n}D_{\rm KL}(p_s^{(\alpha,1)}*\nu\|
                  p_s^{(\alpha,1)}*G_n\nu)\longrightarrow+\infty.
\end{equation}
Consequently, finiteness of the \(2n\)th absolute moment is equivalent to
boundedness of the scaled relative entropy in
\eqref{eq:stable-gaussian-quadrature-finite}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Since \(1+\alpha<2(2n)\), the all-order critical exponent at \(r=2n\) is
\(p_{2n,\alpha,1}=2n\).  Gaussian exactness through degree \(2n-1\) and
\eqref{eq:gauss-missing-moment-norm} show that the first unmatched moment is
\(\|\pi_n\|_{L^2(\nu)}^2\).  Theorem
\ref{thm:all-order-stable-first-unmatched-moment} therefore gives
\eqref{eq:stable-gaussian-quadrature-finite} and
\eqref{eq:stable-gaussian-quadrature-constant}.  If this moment difference
vanishes, \(\nu=G_n\nu\), and the same formula holds with both sides zero.
Strict positivity of \(C_{\alpha,n}\) also follows from the Fourier argument
in that theorem.

For the converse, define
\[
 R_n(u):=(-1)^n\left\{\cos u-
       \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{(-1)^ku^{2k}}{(2k)!}\right\}.
\]
One has \(R_1=1-\cos\ge0\), while
\(R_n''=R_{n-1}\) and \(R_n(0)=R_n'(0)=0\).  Induction therefore gives
\(R_n\ge0\) on \(\RR\).  Moreover,
\(s^{2n}R_n(x/s)\to x^{2n}/(2n)!\).  If the \(2n\)th moment of \(\nu\) is
infinite, Fatou's lemma gives
\[
 s^{2n}\int R_n(x/s)\nu(\dd x)\longrightarrow+\infty.
\]
The corresponding integral for the finite-support law \(G_n\nu\) remains
bounded.  Since all even moments below \(2n\) agree, it follows that
\[
 s^{2n}\left|\Re\{\varphi_\nu(1/s)
                 -\varphi_{G_n\nu}(1/s)\}\right|\longrightarrow+\infty.
\]
At frequency \(1/s\), stable smoothing multiplies this difference by the
fixed nonzero number \(\widehat p_1^{(\alpha,1)}(1)\).  The dual
characterization of total variation and Pinsker's inequality now imply
\eqref{eq:stable-gaussian-quadrature-infinite}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The law-by-law finite-covariance decomposition}

The preceding theorem optimizes over moment classes.  The next theorem gives
the exact law-by-law interface under finite covariance alone.  It separates
the universal quadratic covariance energy from the full nonlinear energy of
the raw tail beyond the smoothing scale.

\begin{theorem}[Stable law-by-law tail decomposition]
\label{thm:stable-law-by-law-decomposition}
Let \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), and let \(\nu\) be a centred probability law
on \(\RR^d\) with finite covariance matrix \(\Sigma\).  Put
\[
 H_{\alpha,d}(s):=
 D_{\rm KL}\!\left(p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu\,\middle\|\,
 p_s^{(\alpha,d)}\right)
\]
and define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-raw-tail-potential}
 V_s^\nu(y):=\int_{\{|x|>s\}}
 \frac{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y-x/s)}
      {p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}\,\nu(\dd x).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-law-by-law-decomposition}
 H_{\alpha,d}(s)=\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)s^{-4}
 +\int_{\RR^d}\Phi(V_s^\nu(y))\,\Omega_{\alpha,d}(\dd y)
 +o(s^{-4}).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-law-by-law-criterion}
 s^4H_{\alpha,d}(s)\longrightarrow\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 s^4\int_{\RR^d}\Phi(V_s^\nu)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
No regular-variation, absolute-continuity, or moment hypothesis above order two
is imposed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For brevity write
\[
 p_1=p_1^{(\alpha,d)},\qquad
 F_y(z)=F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)
 =\frac{p_1(y-z)}{p_1(y)}.
\]
Let \(\ell_y(z)\) and \(B_2(y,z)\) denote the homogeneous first- and
second-order Taylor terms of \(F_y(z)\) at zero.  The estimates in
Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package} and Taylor's formula give, for
\(|z|\le1\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-local-taylor-modulus}
 \|F_\cdot(z)-1-\ell_\cdot(z)-B_2(\cdot,z)\|_\infty
 +\|F_\cdot(z)-1-\ell_\cdot(z)-B_2(\cdot,z)\|_{L^1(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}
 \le\varepsilon_{\alpha,d}(|z|)|z|^2,
\end{equation}
where \(\varepsilon_{\alpha,d}\) is bounded on \([0,1]\) and tends to zero
at zero.  The uniform term is in fact \(O(|z|^3)\).  For the \(L^1\)
term, multiplication by \(p_1(y)\) turns it into the second-order
translation remainder of \(p_1\).  Since \(D^2p_1\in L^1\), the integral
form of Taylor's theorem and translation continuity in \(L^1\) give
\[
 \int_0^1(1-\theta)|z|^2
 \|D^2p_1(\mathord\cdot-\theta z)-D^2p_1\|_1\dd\theta=o(|z|^2).
\]
The Taylor coefficients also satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-taylor-coefficient-norms}
 \|B_j(\cdot,z)\|_\infty
 +\|B_j(\cdot,z)\|_{L^1(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}
 \le C|z|^j,\qquad j=1,2,\quad B_1=\ell.
\end{equation}

Write
\[
 \delta_s(y)=\int\{F_y(x/s)-1\}\nu(\dd x),\qquad
 u_s=s^{-2}b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma},\qquad
 \tau_s=\nu(|x|>s).
\]
Finite covariance implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-tail-mass-smallness}
 \tau_s\le s^{-2}\int_{|x|>s}|x|^2\nu(\dd x)=o(s^{-2}).
\end{equation}
Centering and the identity
\(\int B_2(y,x)\nu(\dd x)=b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}(y)\) give the exact split
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-raw-tail-split}
 \delta_s=u_s+V_s^\nu-\tau_s+R_s,
\end{equation}
where
\[
 R_s=\int_{|x|\le s}\!
 \{F_\cdot(x/s)-1-\ell_\cdot(x/s)-B_2(\cdot,x/s)\}\nu(\dd x)
 -\int_{|x|>s}\!\{\ell_\cdot(x/s)+B_2(\cdot,x/s)\}\nu(\dd x).
\]
Equations \eqref{eq:stable-local-taylor-modulus} and
\eqref{eq:stable-taylor-coefficient-norms}, followed by dominated
convergence after multiplication by \(s^2\), show that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-raw-tail-remainder-smallness}
 \|R_s\|_\infty+\|R_s\|_{L^1(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}=o(s^{-2}).
\end{equation}
For the omitted tail modes one uses
\[
 s^{-1}\int_{|x|>s}|x|\nu(\dd x)
 \le s^{-2}\int_{|x|>s}|x|^2\nu(\dd x)
\]
and the analogous quadratic bound.

The translation identity for \(F_y\) gives the exact normalization
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-tail-potential-normalization}
 V_s^\nu\ge0,\qquad
 \int V_s^\nu\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}=\tau_s.
\end{equation}
All entropy integrals used below are finite.  Indeed,
Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package} and
\(1+|w+z|\le(1+|w|)(1+|z|)\) give
\[
 D_{\rm KL}\!\left(p_1(\mathord\cdot-z)\,\middle\|\,p_1\right)
 \le C_{\alpha,d}+(d+\alpha)\log(1+|z|).
\]
Convexity of relative entropy and \(\EE|X|^2<\infty\) therefore make
\(H_{\alpha,d}(s)\) finite.  If \(\tau_s>0\), write
\(V_s^\nu=\tau_s q_s\), where \(q_s\) is the quotient of the normalized
tail mixture by \(p_1\).  Convexity gives
\[
 \int q_s\log q_s\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
 \le \frac1{\tau_s}\int_{|x|>s}
 \left\{C_{\alpha,d}+(d+\alpha)\log(1+|x|/s)\right\}\nu(\dd x)<\infty.
\]
Since \(\Phi(\tau q)\le\tau q\log(1+q)\) for \(0\le\tau\le1\), and the
negative part of \(q\log q\) is bounded by \(e^{-1}\), this also proves
\(\int\Phi(V_s^\nu)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}<\infty\).  The case \(\tau_s=0\)
is immediate.

For \(|u|\le1/4\) and \(v\ge0\), two integrations of
\(\Phi''(w)=(1+w)^{-1}\) yield
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-phi-interaction}
 |\Phi(u+v)-\Phi(u)-\Phi(v)|\le C|u|v.
\end{equation}
All negative terms in \eqref{eq:stable-raw-tail-split} are uniformly larger
than \(-1/2\) for large \(s\).  The mean-value theorem,
\(\log(1+v)\le v\), and
\eqref{eq:stable-tail-potential-normalization} therefore give
\begin{align}
 \int|\Phi(\delta_s)-\Phi(u_s+V_s^\nu-\tau_s)|
       \dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}&=o(s^{-4}),\label{eq:stable-remove-remainder}\\
 \int|\Phi(u_s+V_s^\nu-\tau_s)-\Phi(u_s+V_s^\nu)|
       \dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}&=o(s^{-4}),\label{eq:stable-remove-mass}\\
 \int|\Phi(u_s+V_s^\nu)-\Phi(u_s)-\Phi(V_s^\nu)|
       \dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}&=o(s^{-4}).\label{eq:stable-remove-interaction}
\end{align}
Indeed, the three left sides are bounded, respectively, by
\[
 C\|R_s\|_\infty\tau_s+Cs^{-2}\|R_s\|_1
 +C\|R_s\|_\infty\|R_s\|_1,
 \quad C\tau_s(\tau_s+s^{-2}),
 \quad C\|u_s\|_\infty\tau_s,
\]
and each is \(o(s^{-4})\).

Finally, integration of the second derivatives in
\eqref{eq:stable-leading-covariance-functional} gives
\(\int b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}=0\).  Boundedness of the
covariance mode then implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-covariance-phi-expansion}
 \int\Phi(u_s)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
 =\frac{s^{-4}}2\int b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}^2\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
 +O(s^{-6})
 =\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)s^{-4}+O(s^{-6}).
\end{equation}
Since \(H_{\alpha,d}(s)=\int\Phi(\delta_s)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}\),
equations \eqref{eq:stable-remove-remainder}--
\eqref{eq:stable-covariance-phi-expansion} prove
\eqref{eq:stable-law-by-law-decomposition}.  The equivalence
\eqref{eq:stable-law-by-law-criterion} follows because the tail energy is
nonnegative.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the decomposition resolves]
When \(d+\alpha\le4\), one has \(p_{\alpha,d}=2\), so every
finite-covariance law makes the tail energy \(o(s^{-4})\) by
Theorem~\ref{thm:high-dimensional-kl-moment-threshold}.  When
\(d+\alpha>4\), finite covariance alone need not do so.  In that regime
\eqref{eq:stable-law-by-law-criterion} is the exact missing law-by-law
condition: it neither replaces the nonlinear tail energy by a moment nor
assumes regular variation.
\end{remark}

The finite-covariance proof above uses positivity of the one-sided raw-tail
potential.  At higher order the natural object is a pair of laws, and the
difference of their raw-tail potentials is signed.  Applying \(\Phi\) to that
difference would therefore neither be well-defined in general nor preserve
nonnegativity.  The following relative \(\Phi\)-energy is the replacement.

\input{sec_two_background_kl_lemma}

\input{sec_abstract_kernel_tail_decomposition}

\begin{corollary}[Stable specialization: arbitrary-order law-by-law tail-defect decomposition]
\label{thm:stable-arbitrary-order-law-by-law-decomposition}
Let \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), and let \(r\ge1\) be an integer.  Let
\(\nu,\eta\) be probability laws on \(\RR^d\) satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:arbitrary-tail-moment-hypotheses}
 m_\gamma(\nu)=m_\gamma(\eta)\quad(|\gamma|<r),
 \qquad
 \int_{\RR^d}|x|^r(\nu+\eta)(\dd x)<\infty.
\end{equation}
For \(\lambda\in\{\nu,\eta\}\), put
\[
 \tau_s^\lambda=\lambda(|x|>s),\qquad
 V_s^\lambda(y)=\int_{\{|x|>s\}}
 F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(x/s)\lambda(\dd x),
\]
and use the moment modes \(B_j^\lambda\) from
\eqref{eq:all-order-stable-moment-modes}.  Their values agree for \(j<r\);
write
\[
 C_{r-1,s}(y)=\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}s^{-j}B_j^\nu(y)
             =\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}s^{-j}B_j^\eta(y),
\]
with an empty sum when \(r=1\), and define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:arbitrary-tail-proxy-quotients}
 A_s^\lambda(y)=1+C_{r-1,s}(y)+V_s^\lambda(y)-\tau_s^\lambda.
\end{equation}
For all sufficiently large \(s\), both \(A_s^\lambda\) are positive,
integrate to one against \(\Omega_{\alpha,d}\), and hence define probability
densities
\[
 k_{r,s}^\lambda(x)=s^{-d}p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(x/s)
                    A_s^\lambda(x/s).
\]
 The explicit nonnegative tail-defect energy
\begin{align}
 \mathcal E_{r,s}(\nu,\eta)
 &:=D_{\rm KL}(k_{r,s}^\nu\|k_{r,s}^\eta)\notag\\
 &=\int_{\RR^d}A_s^\eta
 \Phi\!\left(\frac{A_s^\nu-A_s^\eta}{A_s^\eta}\right)
 \dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
 \label{eq:arbitrary-tail-defect-energy}
\end{align}
is finite, and, with
\(\Delta_r=\int x^{\otimes r}(\nu-\eta)(\dd x)\), one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:arbitrary-tail-defect-decomposition}
 D_{\rm KL}(p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu\|p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\eta)
 =\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d,r}(\Delta_r)s^{-2r}
  +\mathcal E_{r,s}(\nu,\eta)+o(s^{-2r}).
\end{equation}
In particular, law by law,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:arbitrary-tail-defect-criterion}
 s^{2r}D_{\rm KL}(p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu\|p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\eta)
 \longrightarrow\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d,r}(\Delta_r)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 s^{2r}\mathcal E_{r,s}(\nu,\eta)\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
No regular-variation or absolute-continuity hypothesis, and no moment above
order \(r\), is required.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:abstract-positive-tail-jet-kernel} to
\(p=p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\), whose admissibility is verified in
Proposition~\ref{prop:tail-jet-kernel-closure-and-examples}.  Its measure
\(\Omega_p\), translate quotient \(F_y^p\), modes \(B_{p,j}^\lambda\),
proxies \(A_{p,s}^\lambda\), proxy densities \(k_{p,r,s}^\lambda\), and
quadratic form \(\mathcal Q_{p,r}\) are, respectively,
\(\Omega_{\alpha,d}\), \(F_y^{(\alpha,d)}\), \(B_j^\lambda\),
\(A_s^\lambda\), \(k_{r,s}^\lambda\), and
\(\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d,r}\).  Since both proxies have mass one,
\[
 D_{\rm KL}(k_{r,s}^\nu\|k_{r,s}^\eta)
 =\int A_s^\eta
   \Phi\!\left(\frac{A_s^\nu-A_s^\eta}{A_s^\eta}\right)
   \dd\Omega_{\alpha,d},
\]
which identifies \(\mathcal E_{r,s}\).  The abstract theorem now gives
positivity, finiteness, \eqref{eq:arbitrary-tail-defect-decomposition}, and
\eqref{eq:arbitrary-tail-defect-criterion}.  Isotropy gives the
orthogonal invariance of the quadratic form.  The abstract hypotheses use
only the displayed order-\(r\) moment, proving the final sentence.

When \(r=2\), \(\eta=\delta_0\), and \(\nu\) is centred, the identified
energy is \(\int\Phi(V_s^\nu-\tau_s^\nu)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}\), which differs
from the energy in Theorem~\ref{thm:stable-law-by-law-decomposition} by
\(o(s^{-4})\), as shown in \eqref{eq:stable-remove-mass}.
\end{proof}

\section{Relative Entropy Dissipation for Two Stable Heat Flows}
\label{sec:fractional-heat-relative-entropy}

Let \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), and let \((p_t)_{t>0}\) be the
isotropic symmetric \(\alpha\)-stable heat kernel on \(\RR^d\), normalized by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-heat-fourier-normalization}
 \widehat p_t(\xi)=e^{-t|\xi|^\alpha},
 \qquad p_t(x)=t^{-d/\alpha}p_1(t^{-1/\alpha}x).
\end{equation}
Thus \(\partial_t p_t=-(-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}p_t\), where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fractional-laplacian-normalization}
 (-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}\varphi(x)
 =c_{d,\alpha}\operatorname{p.v.}\int_{\RR^d}
 \frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha}}\dd y,
 \qquad
 c_{d,\alpha}
 =\frac{\alpha2^{\alpha-1}
 \Gamma((d+\alpha)/2)}{\pi^{d/2}\Gamma(1-\alpha/2)}.
\end{equation}
The stable-kernel estimates used below are recorded in
Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}.  In particular, with
\(\beta=d+\alpha\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-heat-section-kernel-package}
 p_1(x)\asymp(1+|x|)^{-\beta},\qquad
 |D^kp_1(x)|\lesssim(1+|x|)^{-\beta-k}\quad(k=1,2).
\end{equation}
Put \(S_{\alpha,d}:=\|\nabla\log p_1\|_\infty<\infty\) and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-log-bregman-definition}
 \Lambda(a,b):=a\log\frac ab-a+b,
 \qquad a,b>0.
\end{equation}

The following pilot calculation is stated separately because it is the
point at which the moment domain and the jump singularity first meet.

\begin{lemma}[Stable quotient pilot lemma]
\label{lem:stable-quotient-pilot}
Let \(\lambda\) be a probability measure on \(\RR^d\) with finite
\((d+\alpha)\)-th absolute moment, and set
\[
 Q_t^\lambda(y):=\int_{\RR^d}
 \frac{p_1(y-x/t^{1/\alpha})}{p_1(y)}\,\lambda(\dd x).
\]
For every \(0<a<b<\infty\), there are constants
\(0<c_{a,b,\lambda}\le C_{a,b,\lambda}<\infty\) such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pilot-two-sided-score-bounds}
 c_{a,b,\lambda}\le Q_t^\lambda(y)\le C_{a,b,\lambda},
 \qquad
 |\nabla\log Q_t^\lambda(y)|\le2S_{\alpha,d}
\end{equation}
for all \(t\in[a,b]\) and \(y\in\RR^d\).  If \(\mu,\nu\) are two such
measures, \(t>0\) is fixed, and \(u=Q_t^\mu/Q_t^\nu\), then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pilot-bregman-integral-finite}
 \iint_{\RR^d\times\RR^d}
 \frac{p_1(y)Q_t^\nu(y)\Lambda(u(y),u(z))}
 {|y-z|^{d+\alpha}}\dd z\dd y<\infty.
\end{equation}
No moment margin beyond \(d+\alpha\) is required.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The two-sided density bound in
\eqref{eq:stable-heat-section-kernel-package} and
\(1+|y|\le(1+|y-w|)(1+|w|)\) give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pilot-polynomial-quotient}
 \frac{p_1(y-w)}{p_1(y)}\le C(1+|w|)^\beta.
\end{equation}
With \(w=x/t^{1/\alpha}\) and \(t\ge a\), averaging
\eqref{eq:pilot-polynomial-quotient} gives the upper bound in
\eqref{eq:pilot-two-sided-score-bounds}; this is the only place in the
pilot at which the \(d+\alpha\)-order content of the assumption enters.

Since \(\log p_1\) is \(S_{\alpha,d}\)-Lipschitz,
\[
 \frac{p_1(y-w)}{p_1(y)}\ge e^{-S_{\alpha,d}|w|}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 Q_t^\lambda(y)\ge
 \int e^{-S_{\alpha,d}a^{-1/\alpha}|x|}\lambda(\dd x)>0,
\]
uniformly in \(t\in[a,b]\) and \(y\).  If
\(A_t(y)=\int p_1(y-x/t^{1/\alpha})\lambda(\dd x)\), then differentiation
under the integral and positivity show that
\[
 \nabla\log A_t(y)
 =\frac{\int p_1(y-x/t^{1/\alpha})
 \nabla\log p_1(y-x/t^{1/\alpha})\lambda(\dd x)}{A_t(y)}.
\]
Its norm is at most \(S_{\alpha,d}\), and subtracting
\(\nabla\log p_1(y)\) proves the score bound.

For the last assertion, the preceding bounds give constants
\(0<m\le u\le M<\infty\), while
\(|\nabla\log u|\le4S_{\alpha,d}\).  Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pilot-u-lipschitz}
 |u(y)-u(z)|\le4MS_{\alpha,d}|y-z|.
\end{equation}
Taylor's theorem for \(r\mapsto r\log r-r\), whose second derivative is
\(1/r\), gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pilot-lambda-quadratic}
 0\le\Lambda(r,s)\le\frac{|r-s|^2}{2m}
 \qquad(r,s\in[m,M]).
\end{equation}
Thus the integrand in \eqref{eq:pilot-bregman-integral-finite}, without its
probability weight, is bounded by \(C|y-z|^{2-d-\alpha}\) when
\(|y-z|\le1\), and by \(C|y-z|^{-d-\alpha}\) when
\(|y-z|>1\).  Both kernels are integrable in the \(z\)-variable because
\(\alpha<2\) and \(\alpha>0\).  Finally,
\(p_1(y)Q_t^\nu(y)\dd y\) is a probability measure.  Tonelli's theorem
proves \eqref{eq:pilot-bregman-integral-finite}.
\end{proof}

Here is the field-facing consequence.  It concerns two simultaneous
fractional heat flows and does not use the proxy or coefficient terminology
of the other sections.

\begin{theorem}[Relative entropy dissipation for two symmetric stable heat flows]
\label{thm:two-stable-heat-flow-relative-entropy}
Let \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), and use the normalization
\eqref{eq:stable-heat-fourier-normalization}--
\eqref{eq:fractional-laplacian-normalization}.  Let \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) be
probability measures on \(\RR^d\) satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-flow-moment-hypothesis}
 \int_{\RR^d}|x|^{d+\alpha}\mu(\dd x)
 +\int_{\RR^d}|x|^{d+\alpha}\nu(\dd x)<\infty.
\end{equation}
For \(t>0\), define
\[
 f_t=p_t*\mu,\qquad g_t=p_t*\nu,\qquad
 u_t=\frac{f_t}{g_t},\qquad
 H(t)=D_{\rm KL}(f_t\|g_t),
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-flow-dissipation-definition}
 I_{\alpha,d}(t):=c_{d,\alpha}
 \iint_{\RR^d\times\RR^d}
 \frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha}}
 \dd y\dd x.
\end{equation}
Then all of the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For every compact interval \([a,b]\subset(0,\infty)\), there are
constants
\[
 0<m_{a,b}\le M_{a,b}<\infty,\qquad L_{a,b}<\infty,
\]
such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-flow-compact-window-domain}
 m_{a,b}\le u_t(x)\le M_{a,b},\qquad
 |\nabla\log u_t(x)|\le L_{a,b}
\end{equation}
for all \(t\in[a,b]\) and \(x\in\RR^d\).

\item The quantity \(I_{\alpha,d}(t)\) is finite for every \(t>0\) and is
locally integrable on \((0,\infty)\).

\item The function \(H\) is locally absolutely continuous on
\((0,\infty)\), and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-flow-debruijn-identity}
 H'(t)=-I_{\alpha,d}(t)
\end{equation}
for almost every \(t>0\).

\item One has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-flow-w1-decay}
 H(t)\le S_{\alpha,d}t^{-1/\alpha}W_1(\mu,\nu),
\end{equation}
and consequently \(H(t)\to0\) as \(t\to\infty\).

\item For every \(t>0\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-flow-tail-integral}
 D_{\rm KL}(p_t*\mu\|p_t*\nu)
 =\int_t^\infty I_{\alpha,d}(s)\dd s.
\end{equation}

\item There is also a stable-reference version.  Let \(s_0>0\), let
\(\mu\) be a probability measure with finite \((d+\alpha)\)-th absolute
moment, and put
\[
 f_q=p_q*\mu,\qquad g_q=p_{q+s_0},\qquad q>0.
\]
The conclusions in \textup{(ii)} and \textup{(iii)}, and the tail identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-reference-tail-integral}
 D_{\rm KL}(p_q*\mu\|p_{q+s_0})
 =\int_q^\infty I_{\alpha,d}^{(s_0)}(r)\dd r,
\end{equation}
hold with this pair, where \(I_{\alpha,d}^{(s_0)}\) is
\eqref{eq:stable-flow-dissipation-definition} with \(g_r=p_{r+s_0}\).
If \(\mu\) has a density and
\(D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|p_{s_0})<\infty\), then
\begin{align}
 D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|p_{s_0})
 &=c_{d,\alpha}\int_0^\infty
 \iint_{\RR^d\times\RR^d}
 \frac{p_{q+s_0}(x)}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha}}\notag\\
 &\qquad\times
 \Lambda\left(
 \frac{(p_q*\mu)(x)}{p_{q+s_0}(x)},
 \frac{(p_q*\mu)(y)}{p_{q+s_0}(y)}
 \right)\dd y\dd x\dd q.\label{eq:stable-reference-integral-representation}
\end{align}
In dimension one, let \(X\sim\mu\), let \(Z_{s_0}^{(\alpha)}\) be
independent of \(X\) with density \(p_{s_0}\), and let \(h_t\) be the density
of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-stable-interpolation}
 X_t=(1-t)^{1/\alpha}X+t^{1/\alpha}Z_{s_0}^{(\alpha)},
 \qquad 0<t<1.
\end{equation}
Writing \(v_t=h_t/p_{s_0}\), the change of variables
\(q=s_0t/(1-t)\) turns
\eqref{eq:stable-reference-integral-representation} into
\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-stable-interpolation-representation}
 D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|p_{s_0})
 =c_{1,\alpha}s_0\int_0^1\frac1{1-t}
 \iint_{\RR^2}
 \frac{p_{s_0}(x)\Lambda(v_t(x),v_t(y))}
 {|x-y|^{1+\alpha}}\dd y\dd x\dd t.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

We first isolate the noncompact Green-pairing fact used in the proof.  It is
the step for which cancellation at infinity cannot be replaced by a formal
generator calculation.

\begin{lemma}[Annular fractional Green closure]
\label{lem:annular-fractional-green-closure}
For \(0<\varepsilon<1<R\), define
\[
 A_{\varepsilon,R}\varphi(x)
 :=c_{d,\alpha}\int_{\varepsilon<|x-y|<R}
 \frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha}}\dd y.
\]
If \(\varphi\in W^{2,1}(\RR^d)\), then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-generator-l1-limit}
 A_{\varepsilon,R}\varphi\longrightarrow
 (-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}\varphi
 \quad\hbox{in }L^1(\RR^d)
\end{equation}
as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) and \(R\uparrow\infty\).  If
\(\psi\in L^\infty(\RR^d)\), then at every finite annulus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-annulus-green-formula}
 \int\psi A_{\varepsilon,R}\varphi
 =\frac{c_{d,\alpha}}2
 \iint_{\varepsilon<|x-y|<R}
 \frac{(\varphi(x)-\varphi(y))(\psi(x)-\psi(y))}
 {|x-y|^{d+\alpha}}\dd y\dd x.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Symmetry in the increment \(h\) writes the small-jump part in terms of
\(2\varphi(x)-\varphi(x+h)-\varphi(x-h)\).  The integral form of the
second-order Taylor remainder yields
\[
 \|2\varphi-\varphi(\mathord\cdot+h)
 -\varphi(\mathord\cdot-h)\|_1
 \le |h|^2\|D^2\varphi\|_1.
\]
Hence the omitted ball of radius \(\varepsilon\) is bounded in \(L^1\) by
\[
 C\|D^2\varphi\|_1\int_0^\varepsilon r^{1-\alpha}\dd r
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
The omitted region \(|h|>R\) is bounded by
\(C\|\varphi\|_1\int_R^\infty r^{-1-\alpha}\dd r\to0\).
This proves \eqref{eq:annular-generator-l1-limit}, first on smooth
functions and then on \(W^{2,1}\) by the same estimates.  On a finite
annulus all terms are absolutely integrable because \(\varphi\in L^1\) and
\(\psi\) is bounded.  Exchanging \(x\) and \(y\) in one copy of the
integral proves \eqref{eq:finite-annulus-green-formula}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:two-stable-heat-flow-relative-entropy}]
Write \(x=t^{1/\alpha}y\).  The scaling in
\eqref{eq:stable-heat-fourier-normalization} gives
\[
 \frac{f_t(t^{1/\alpha}y)}{p_t(t^{1/\alpha}y)}=Q_t^\mu(y),
 \qquad
 \frac{g_t(t^{1/\alpha}y)}{p_t(t^{1/\alpha}y)}=Q_t^\nu(y).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:stable-quotient-pilot} therefore gives the two-sided bounds
in \eqref{eq:stable-flow-compact-window-domain}.  It also gives
\[
 |\nabla_x\log u_t(x)|
 \le4S_{\alpha,d}t^{-1/\alpha}
 \le4S_{\alpha,d}a^{-1/\alpha},
\]
which proves \textup{(i)}.

On a fixed compact time window, write \(m,M,L\) for the constants in
\eqref{eq:stable-flow-compact-window-domain}.  Since
\(|\nabla u_t|\le ML\), \eqref{eq:pilot-lambda-quadratic} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-flow-bregman-majorant}
 0\le\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))\le
 C\min\{|x-y|^2,1\}.
\end{equation}
The constant is uniform on the window.  Integrating first in \(y\) and then
against the probability density \(g_t(x)\) proves that
\(I_{\alpha,d}(t)\) is finite and locally bounded.  This proves
\textup{(ii)} and also supplies an integrable majorant for every annular
cutoff below.

The derivative estimate in
\eqref{eq:stable-heat-section-kernel-package}, together with scaling, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-kernel-relative-time-derivative}
 |\partial_t p_t(x)|\le C_{d,\alpha}t^{-1}p_t(x).
\end{equation}
Indeed, differentiating \(t^{-d/\alpha}p_1(t^{-1/\alpha}x)\) reduces this to
the boundedness of
\(|y||\nabla p_1(y)|/p_1(y)\).  Convolution gives the same relative bound
for \(f_t\) and \(g_t\).  The compact quotient range then permits
differentiation of the pointwise entropy integrand.  On
\([a,b]\times\RR^d\), the absolute value of that derivative is bounded by
\(C(f_t+g_t)\), whose space-time integral is \(2C(b-a)\).  Fubini's theorem
and the one-dimensional fundamental theorem for absolutely continuous
functions therefore give local absolute continuity of \(H\) and, for almost
every \(t\), the stable-kernel identity can be used in \(L^1\).  Indeed,
convolving \(\partial_t p_t=-Ap_t\), where
\(A=(-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}\), with the initial probability measures gives
\(Af_t=-\partial_t f_t\) and \(Ag_t=-\partial_t g_t\) in \(L^1\).  Hence
\begin{align}
 H'(t)
 &=\int_{\RR^d}\log u_t\,\partial_t f_t\dd x
 -\int_{\RR^d}(u_t-1)\partial_tg_t\dd x\notag\\
 &=-\int\log u_t\,Af_t+\int(u_t-1)Ag_t\notag\\
 &=-\int\log u_t\,Af_t+\int u_t\,Ag_t.
 \label{eq:stable-flow-l1-chain-rule}
\end{align}
Indeed, \(\int A_{\varepsilon,R}g_t\dd x=0\) on every finite annulus,
and the \(L^1\) convergence in
Lemma~\ref{lem:annular-fractional-green-closure} therefore gives
\(\int Ag_t\dd x=0\).  This also proves local absolute continuity directly.

For each fixed \(t>0\), stable smoothing gives
\(f_t,g_t\in W^{2,1}(\RR^d)\).  Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:annular-fractional-green-closure} first with
\((\varphi,\psi)=(f_t,\log u_t)\) and then with
\((\varphi,\psi)=(g_t,u_t)\).  The two individual left sides converge by
\eqref{eq:annular-generator-l1-limit}, because \(u_t\) and
\(\log u_t\) are bounded.  At a finite annulus their difference is
\begin{align*}
 &-\frac{c_{d,\alpha}}2\iint
 \frac{(g_xu_x-g_yu_y)(\log u_x-\log u_y)
 -(g_x-g_y)(u_x-u_y)}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha}}\dd y\dd x\\
 &=-\frac{c_{d,\alpha}}2\iint
 \frac{g_x\Lambda(u_x,u_y)+g_y\Lambda(u_y,u_x)}
 {|x-y|^{d+\alpha}}\dd y\dd x,
\end{align*}
where the integrations are over
\(\varepsilon<|x-y|<R\).  Exchanging \(x,y\) in the second summand makes
this the negative of the one-sided annular version of
\eqref{eq:stable-flow-dissipation-definition}.  The majorant
\eqref{eq:stable-flow-bregman-majorant} removes both annular cutoffs by
dominated convergence.  Thus both noncompact Green pairings close
separately and
\(H'(t)=-I_{\alpha,d}(t)\).  No cancellation has been invoked before the
two \(L^1\) generator limits exist.  This proves \textup{(iii)}.

For any coupling \(\pi\) of \(\mu\) and \(\nu\), joint convexity of relative
entropy and the Lipschitz bound for \(\log p_t\) give
\begin{align*}
 H(t)
 &\le\int D_{\rm KL}
 \bigl(p_t(\mathord\cdot-x)\|p_t(\mathord\cdot-y)\bigr)
 \pi(\dd x,\dd y)\\
 &\le S_{\alpha,d}t^{-1/\alpha}
 \int|x-y|\pi(\dd x,\dd y).
\end{align*}
Taking the infimum over \(\pi\) proves \eqref{eq:stable-flow-w1-decay}.
The moment hypothesis implies finite first moments, so the right side tends
to zero.  This is \textup{(iv)}.  Integrating
\eqref{eq:stable-flow-debruijn-identity} from \(t\) to \(T\), and then using
nonnegativity and \(H(T)\to0\), proves \textup{(v)}.

It remains to treat the stable reference.  On every compact \(q\)-window,
the quotient \((p_q*\mu)/p_q\) has the bounds in the pilot lemma.  The ratio
\(p_{q+s_0}/p_q\) and its reciprocal are uniformly bounded there by
\eqref{eq:stable-heat-section-kernel-package} and scaling; their logarithmic
gradients are uniformly bounded as well.  Hence the compact-window proof
above applies to \(f_q=p_q*\mu\), \(g_q=p_{q+s_0}\), even though the stable
law \(p_{s_0}\dd x\) need not have a \((d+\alpha)\)-moment.

For any \(q_0>0\), the corresponding quotient \(f_q/g_q\) is bounded above
and below uniformly for all \(q\ge q_0\).  Moreover,
\begin{align*}
 \|p_q*\mu-p_q\|_1
 &\le\int\|p_1(\mathord\cdot-x/q^{1/\alpha})-p_1\|_1\mu(\dd x)
 \longrightarrow0,\\
 \|p_{q+s_0}-p_q\|_1&\longrightarrow0.
\end{align*}
The first limit is dominated convergence and \(L^1\)-translation
continuity; the second is \(L^1\)-continuity of dilations.  On a fixed
compact quotient range, \(r\log r-r+1\le C|r-1|\).  Therefore
\(D_{\rm KL}(p_q*\mu\|p_{q+s_0})\to0\), which proves
\eqref{eq:stable-reference-tail-integral} by the already established local
identity.

Suppose now that the initial relative entropy is finite.  Convolution by
\(p_q\) is a Markov kernel, so data processing gives
\[
 D_{\rm KL}(p_q*\mu\|p_q*p_{s_0})
 \le D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|p_{s_0}).
\]
As \(q\downarrow0\), both arguments on the left converge weakly to the
corresponding arguments on the right.  Lower semicontinuity of relative
entropy supplies the reverse liminf inequality.  Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-reference-small-time-kl-limit}
 D_{\rm KL}(p_q*\mu\|p_{q+s_0})
 \longrightarrow D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|p_{s_0}).
\end{equation}
Letting \(q\downarrow0\) in
\eqref{eq:stable-reference-tail-integral} and using monotone convergence
proves \eqref{eq:stable-reference-integral-representation}.

Finally set \(r=(1-t)^{1/\alpha}\) and
\(q=s_0t/(1-t)\).  The density in
\eqref{eq:johnson-stable-interpolation} and the stable reference satisfy
\[
 h_t(x)=r^{-1}(p_q*\mu)(x/r),\qquad
 p_{s_0}(x)=r^{-1}p_{q+s_0}(x/r).
\]
Thus \(v_t(x)=u_q(x/r)\).  The spatial change of variables in the jump form
gives \(I_{\alpha,1}^{(s_0)}(q)=(1-t)\) times the double integral in
\eqref{eq:johnson-stable-interpolation-representation}, while
\(\dd q=s_0(1-t)^{-2}\dd t\).  This proves that representation and
completes \textup{(vi)}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Domain and novelty boundary]
\label{rem:stable-flow-domain-novelty-boundary}
The exponent \(d+\alpha\) is a transparent sufficient hypothesis, not an
optimality claim.  It is natural here because the stable tail has precisely
that exponent and the worst-case translate quotient in
\eqref{eq:pilot-polynomial-quotient} grows like
\((1+|x|)^{d+\alpha}\).  The \(d+\alpha\)-order content of the hypothesis
enters only in the uniform upper quotient bound; the lower quotient bound
uses much less.  The hypothesis is also used in \textup{(iv)} through its
finite-first-moment consequence, which makes \(W_1(\mu,\nu)\) finite, but
that endpoint step does not use the \(d+\alpha\) exponent.  It remains open
here whether the dissipation identity holds under finite first moment,
finite initial relative entropy, or a direct Dirichlet-form domain condition.

The two-point logarithmic algebra is not new.  Broad Hardy--Stein,
polarized, nonlinear Douglas, and Sobolev--Bregman identities for pure-jump
forms are already available
\cite{BanuelosBogdanLuks2016HardyStein,Gutowski2023HardySteinPureJump,
BogdanGrzywnyPietruskaPalubaRutkowski2023NonlinearNonlocalDouglas,
GutowskiKwasnicki2025BeurlingDenySobolevBregman,
BogdanGutowskiPietruskaPaluba2025PolarizedHardyStein}; conditional
Hardy--Stein identities also treat ratios of harmonic functions and general
convex functions \cite{KlimsiakRozkosz2025ConditionalHardyStein}.  For two
positive solutions of the same forward Kolmogorov equation on a finite or
countable state space, Hilder--Peletier--Sharma--Tse write the corresponding
one-sided Bregman sum and trace entropy contraction to Voigt's stochastic-
operator theorem
\cite{HilderPeletierSharmaTse2020EntropyDistance,Voigt1981StochasticOperators}.
Gaussian moving-reference de Bruijn identities and an integral
representation also precede the present work
\cite{HirataNemotoYoshida2012IntegralRepresentation}.  The claim of
Theorem~\ref{thm:two-stable-heat-flow-relative-entropy} is therefore the
stable-continuum measure-data domain and endpoint theorem for the classical
two-solution entropy-production identity, including the separate noncompact
Green pairings.  We provide an exact nonlocal Bregman integral representation
along Johnson's symmetric-stable interpolation, under the stated
finite-moment and finite-initial-entropy domain; we do not identify the
integrand with Johnson's score pairing in
\cite[Theorem~5.1]{Johnson2013StableDeBruijn}.  The theorem does not extend
to all isotropic unimodal L\'evy semigroups or all subordinate Brownian
motions.
\end{remark}
